extracted.intended_audience: Authors and teams preparing Cochrane systematic reviews of interventions (review authors, editors, and methodologists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for starting and planning Cochrane intervention systematic reviews, including question formulation, protocol development and registration, team composition and conflicts of interest, search planning, risk-of-bias assessment, synthesis planning (including meta-analysis and GRADE), stakeholder involvement, and data management/quality assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-specify research question and methods (a priori specification)
rubrics_metrics.description: A systematic review attempts to collate all empirical evidence that fits pre-specified eligibility criteria in order to answer a specific research question; the a priori specification of a research question and methods is central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For questions about effects, use the PICO approach (Population, Intervention, Comparison(s), Outcome). The review question should determine the methods used (not vice versa). Question formulation should be informed by wide input from relevant perspectives so the review addresses an important question for expected users. See Chapter 2 for detailed formulation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team-based conduct and independent assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic reviews should be undertaken by a team; Cochrane will not publish a review proposed to be undertaken by a single person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teams spread effort and ensure key tasks (selection for eligibility, data extraction, rating certainty) are performed by at least two people independently to minimize errors. First-time authors should work with experienced colleagues and receive training. Teams should include both topic and methodological/statistical expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of topic and methodological expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Review teams must include expertise in the topic area and systematic review methodology, including statistical expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topic expertise should not be overly narrow; both topic and methodological expertise together provide insight into implementation, condition nature, outcome relationships, and other decision-relevant factors. While methodological expertise alone has been argued for, a mix of skills, knowledge and objectivity is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest management
rubrics_metrics.description: A Cochrane review should represent an independent assessment of the evidence; avoiding financial and non-financial conflicts of interest often requires careful management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should consult the Conflict of Interest Policy. Funding of Cochrane reviews by commercial organizations with an interest in the outcome is not permitted. Authors must make complete declarations of interest before registration, refresh these annually until publication and just prior to publication, and update declarations whenever circumstances change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer and stakeholder involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: People who might make or be affected by decisions should be involved in important review decisions; consumers are joint partners in research from planning to dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map potential stakeholders (patients, carers, policy makers, guideline developers, practitioners, funders, journalists, etc.), balance seniority and diversity, consider resource-poor settings and marginalized groups. Methods include surveys, workshops, focus groups, advisory groups. Provide support (training, reimbursement), use terms of reference/job descriptions, coordinate advisory group input throughout the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability and auditability of reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic reviews aim to be an accurate representation of current knowledge and need to be accurate at publication because decisions (including legal/regulatory) may be based on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should use detailed evidence-based methods, provide transparent reporting to aid auditability, and be prepared so that they can be scrutinized and held up to legal examination when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to MECIR expectations (conduct and reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cochrane has developed methodological expectations for conduct, reporting and updating of reviews (MECIR) and plain language summaries; each expectation has a title, rationale and elaboration and is classified as 'mandatory' or 'highly desirable'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandatory items are expected to be applied or require justification if not implemented (failure may be basis for non-publication in CDSR). Highly desirable items should generally be implemented though exceptions exist. MECIR expectations are presented across Handbook chapters; reporting expectations incorporate PRISMA recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protocol development and registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods to be used in the review should be established and documented in advance in a protocol; publication and registration of protocols is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A protocol reduces bias, promotes transparency, reduces duplication, allows peer review of planned methods, and helps plan resources. Protocols should define eligibility criteria, planned analyses (including variability investigations), and methods for interpreting results. Protocols should be published (Cochrane Protocols in CDSR) and registered on PROSPERO. Changes to protocols are sometimes necessary but should not be made based on knowledge of study findings and must be transparently declared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning the search (MECIR C19 — Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan in advance the methods to be used for identifying studies. Design searches to capture as many studies as possible that meet the eligibility criteria, ensuring relevant time periods and sources are covered and not restricted by language or publication status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searches should be motivated by the eligibility criteria and consider all types of eligible studies. Restricting searches by publication status or language risks publication or language bias. Removing language restrictions in English databases is not a substitute for searching non-English databases. Searching may need to include unpublished sources to reduce reporting bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning assessment of risk of bias in included studies (MECIR C20 — Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan in advance the methods to be used for assessing risk of bias in included studies, including the tool(s), how they'll be implemented, and criteria for assigning judgments (low/unclear/high risk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predefining methods and criteria is important because subsequent analysis/interpretation may be affected by these judgments. For randomized trials, using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool is Mandatory; refer to Handbook definitions of low/unclear/high risk of bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning the synthesis of results (MECIR C21 — Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan in advance the methods for synthesizing results, including whether quantitative synthesis is planned, how heterogeneity will be assessed, choice of effect measure, and methods for meta-analysis (e.g. inverse variance or Mantel–Haenszel, fixed-effect or random-effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predefining synthesis and statistical methods is important because analysis or interpretation can be affected by post hoc choices. Specify effect measures (odds ratio, risk ratio, risk difference, etc.) and analytic approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning subgroup analyses (MECIR C22 — Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Predefine potential effect modifiers for subgroup analyses at the protocol stage; restrict these analyses in number and provide a rationale for each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-specification reduces the risk that many undirected subgroup analyses will lead to spurious explanations of heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning GRADE assessment and 'Summary of findings' table (MECIR C23 — Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan in advance the methods for assessing the certainty of the body of evidence and summarizing the review findings; predefine choice of important outcomes for the 'Summary of findings' table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-specify methods for assessing certainty (e.g. GRADE). The 'Summary of findings' should include essential outcomes for decision making (typically up to seven), generally not surrogate or interim outcomes. Outcome choice should not be based on anticipated or observed magnitude of effect or because they are likely to have been addressed in included studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid post hoc decisions and selective reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to protocols or analysis decisions should not be made on the basis of their effect on results; post hoc decisions (e.g., excluding selected studies, changing statistical analysis after seeing results) are highly susceptible to bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some changes may be necessary for legitimate reasons, they must be transparently declared and justified. Public availability of protocols and registration reduce potential for selective reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data management and quality assurance (audit trail and reproducibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic reviews should be replicable; retain records of inclusion decisions, data collection, transformations or adjustments to establish a secure and retrievable audit trail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use review management software (e.g., Covidence, EPPI-Reviewer) to assist data management and standardize records. Maintain independent assessments of inclusion, risk of bias, and data extraction. Quality assurance is essential (even though it costs author time) because reviewers make mistakes and disagree. Store review data to facilitate updates and enable semi-automation or machine-learning-assisted updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic review as prerequisite to new primary research
rubrics_metrics.description: New research should typically be designed or commissioned only if it does not unnecessarily duplicate existing research; systematic reviews should typically be undertaken before embarking on new primary research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A systematic review identifies current and ongoing studies and gaps in knowledge, reveals limitations of prior studies that new research might address, and helps avoid research waste and unnecessary duplication.
